items.title: Fed keeps rates on hold despite inflation surge; ASX set to rise, Wall Street advances

Share A A A Wall Street is steady after the Federal Reserve announced it will keep interest rates on hold.
It was a widely expected move, with the central bank opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week’s US midterm elections and awaiting further data on the path of inflation.

Fed chair Kevin Warsh said the central bank has “started to see some changes in financial and credit conditions. They have tightened for some businesses and households.” Bloomberg The S&P 500 rose 0.2 per cent and pulled within 1 per cent of its all-time high, which was set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 149 points, or 0.3 per cent, in mid-afternoon trade and the Nasdaq composite was mostly unchanged.

The Australian sharemarket is set to climb, with futures at 5.05am AEDT pointing to a rise of 24 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The ASX closed flat on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.35¢.

In a 10-2 decision, the Fed said it would maintain its benchmark interest rate within the current 3.75 per cent-4.00 per cent range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated,” upgrading its assessment of the economy, and hinting that further rate hikes may be coming depending on the performance of inflation.

“The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 per cent goal,” the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee said in its latest policy statement. “The Committee will deliver price stability.”
At a news conference following the announcement, Warsh said the Fed has “started to see some changes in financial and credit conditions. They have tightened for some businesses and households.”

The Fed raised its benchmark rate last month for the first time in three years, defying President Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts, in an effort to get inflation back to its 2 per cent target in a “timelier” manner. The Fed is tasked by Congress to combat inflation, and it does so by lifting rates to slow borrowing and spending and cool price increases. The statement leaves the Fed’s next moves unclear, even though officials last month penciled in another rate hike for this year. Wall Street investors have also priced in a rate hike in December, according to futures markets.

Fed Governor Lisa Cook, currently targeted by President Donald Trump for removal from the central bank, dissented in favour of a quarter-percentage-point rate hike, as did Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, a consistently hawkish voice who also dissented in July for the same reason

Wall Street cares so much about interest rates because they are one of the main levers that set prices for stocks. The other big variable is how much profit companies are making, and several companies rallied Wednesday after joining the list of those beating analysts’ expectations for the summer.

Wall Street held its gains after the widely-expected decision and Warsh’s press conference. Bloomberg GE HealthCare Technologies jumped 7.2 per cent after delivering both profit and revenue for the summer that surpassed analysts’ expectations. It also raised its forecasts for revenue growth and other financial measures for the full year.

Etsy climbed 5.3 per cent after its profit for the latest quarter blew past analysts’ forecasts. CEO Kruti Patel Goyal said the online marketplace saw growth in active buyers from prior-year levels for the first time in two years, while its active seller base grew at its fastest rate in two years.

Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry were also relatively solid. They’ve stabilised this week following big swings on worries that high borrowing costs caused by high interest rates will undercut the boom in AI data centres largely built with borrowed money.

AI stocks got an additional boost after a major player in the industry, South Korea’s SK Hynix, soared 10.9 per cent in Seoul following its latest profit report. The seller of memory chips said it’s in the midst of a virtuous cycle of rising AI usage, and it expects demand to continue to outpace supply through 2030.
On Wall Street, Micron Technology rose 4.7 per cent and was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500. It also sells memory for computers.
Outside of tech and earnings, Wendy’s soared 15.1 per cent to $US7.09 after Trian Fund Management, run by investor Nelson Peltz, offered to buy the chain for $US7.35 per share in cash.

That helped offset a drop for Boston Scientific, which fell 5 per cent even though the seller of medical devices reported a milder drop in profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for profit in the current quarter that fell short of analysts’ expectations.
Robinhood Markets sank 4.2 per cent after reporting weaker profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected.
In the bond market, Treasury yields ticked higher, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 5.03 per cent from 4.99 per cent late Tuesday.

It’s near the high end of its range since shooting upward from 3.97 per cent when the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation much higher. But it’s pulled back after topping 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touching its highest level since 2002.

Rising oil prices pushed upward on Treasury yields Wednesday as uncertainty continues about what will happen in the Middle East and the global energy industry. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, climbed 2.7 per cent to $US112.39.
In stock markets abroad, South Korea’s Kospi jumped 6.6 per cent following SK Hynix’s leap. Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 1.1 per cent, while France’s CAC 40 rose 0.1 per cent.

items.title: Bathla offered top dollar for land, but some sellers fought to be paid
paras: Bathla Group bought a parcel in Box Hill from Michael Ryan for $39.5 million. It missed settlement dates, so Ryan financed part of the sale.

Legal records show Bathla, through subsidiaries, failed to secure funding on three separate property transactions totaling about $130 million. The delays, attributed to rapid expansion, left the company vulnerable when the market cooled, prompting court‑ordered payments. Sellers now face higher risks when buyers rely on external financing, potentially reshaping future property deals.
Keep an eye on court rulings that could tighten buyer financing protocols.
items.impact: When Michael Ryan agreed to sell his sprawling property in Sydney's north-west for $39.5 million, it is unlikely he expected a protracted legal battle to get the buyer to pay.

items.title: Bad inflation result lays bare the ugly truth: There is no easy way out
paras: Jim Chalmers and Anthony Albanese are caught in a political bind when it comes to inflation. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )
It is hard to imagine after nearly five years of economic pain, but the grim truth revealed by yesterday's batch of high inflation numbers is inescapable: the worst is yet to come.

Most observers now think the Reserve Bank will hike rates again on Tuesday. That would take the cash rate to 4.85 per cent, its highest level in 18 years. By now, we know this means a tighter financial squeeze for all borrowers.

Few will want to spare a thought for the politicians, but the news also piled on the agony for Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who had to front up once again for a stony-faced press conference and a Question Time laden with jeers from the opposition benches.

As he has done countless times, Chalmers acknowledged those "doing it tough" and solemnly swore the government would continue to be "responsible". And, as always, he snarled at "commentators" who say public spending is the root cause of the problem.

He might have a point. The role of global events is obvious, and is pushing up inflation all over the world. And a private sector investment boom, propelled by the rush to build data centres, hasn't helped either. They're excuses, but they're real ones.
Still, how many times can you reassure people that you're doing everything you can and that you're sensitive to the difficulty they're enduring before your words lose weight?
The answer: you can keep it up for as long as you can sell hope. And that's getting tough.

Rewind to 2022, when this inflation episode began, and hope was a carefully calibrated part of the message. The government and the Reserve Bank were singing from the same song sheet, promising a relatively painless route out of trouble.

They called it "the narrow path to a soft landing". Interest rates would go up, but not as harshly as in other countries. They might stay high for a little longer, but without doing excessive damage to the jobs market or the broader economy in the process.
Was the plan to tackle inflation, supported by RBA governor Michele Bullock, too good to be true? ( ABC News: John Gunn )

There were always those who said this sounded too good to be true. Inflation has wrought havoc whenever it has taken hold in history, and it has rarely been possible to banish it without a recession, such as the one Paul Keating said we "had to have" in 1990.

But it was an admirable ambition, and it's not entirely anyone's fault that it didn't work out. Yes, the "narrow path" strategy probably was the reason why Australia had more heat left in inflation when the war hit. But that's why it was called "narrow".

And the war, coupled with the AI investment boom, have made for a perfect storm not just in Australia but in other countries, too. The boom pushed up demand, and the war constrained what could be supplied, stretching out the gap where inflation thrives.

That is the simple and ruthless logic of inflation. When demand in an economy outstrips what can be supplied, inflation is the result, because the excess demand has nowhere to go other than to bid prices up.

To stamp that out, all that can be done is to slash demand or expand our capacity for supply. The latter option is what economists mean when they talk about productivity. Sluggish productivity growth is what Michele Bullock calls our "fundamental challenge".

But, in the meantime, the only other option is to slash demand, from anywhere. Rate hikes do this by slugging borrowers. Critics who say they do not address the root cause of inflation misunderstand the aim; it might be unfair, but it can be effective.
Dealing with inflation will put further pressure on everyday households. ( ABC News: Tristan Hooft )
The government can also reduce demand, either by cutting spending or hiking taxes. These can be more targeted approaches, but the political difficulties are obvious.

That is why economists like Chris Richardson tend not to ask governments to slash and burn, and instead judge them by the precautionary principle: at the very least, don't make things worse by spending more or handing out large tax cuts.

Of course, that is exactly what governments are tempted to do when voters are worn down by all those high prices. And, as Chalmers put it on Tuesday, helping people with the cost of living can be legitimate and necessary. It's an exercise in "balance".

As the opposition has pointed out, the government could have been a little braver if it wanted to. Spending like the EV discount and the home batteries discount might have achieved a climate goal but has put billions into the pockets of high-income earners.

But these are small in the grand scheme of things. And as the government points out, nobody in politics wants to identify acceptable spending cuts on a grander scale. It's hard to argue that a subsidy here or there is the main reason we are where we are.

Anyway, that sort of quibbling dodges the ugly truth about what lies ahead. The Reserve Bank, with the government's support, tried to get rid of inflation without triggering job losses and a recession. The soft approach didn't work.

That means that narrow path, and that soft landing, are likely beyond us. We have escaped the worst until now, with minimal change in the jobs market and minimal business closures or distressed housing sales.
Absent a productivity boom, which nobody can clearly articulate how to create, we will be going harder for longer, suppressing demand well into 2027.

That will happen with higher rates, and it will probably happen on the budget balance sheet too. For all his defensiveness about the role of government spending, Chalmers has promised further savings and poured cold water on calls for cost-of-living relief.
Around the cabinet table and the RBA board table is a shared recognition: that inflation is destructive, that it is making people angry, but that the only way is through.

items.title: Ten things to look out for in the Budget
paras: It’s Budget day. The run-up to Andy Burnham and John Healey’s first fiscal event has been rather less eventful than last year. There’ve been no daily leaks, no pitch-rolling press conferences and no hysteria. Everything that’s trickled out to the papers over the last few days has been small beer.

So we have a mystery: will this Budget be trick, treat, both or neither? If what Healey unveils to the House of Commons just after 12.30 today proves small in terms of spending and revenue, the Treasury team will be briefing that this was prudence rather than boring. With economic growth tentatively coming back to life so far this year, and following two Reeves Budgets which hiked taxes by a record £75 billion, they know there is little room for anything big.

Healey’s overall aim is for his Budget to give ‘breathing space for businesses and households’. What that is likely to mean is small measures paid for by small tax rises on banks, bookies and big businesses. One such measure was already announced this morning: the scrapping of standing charges on gas bills. That will be paid for by increasing the unit charge on gas charges but it brings bills down because it rewards efficiency in gas usage. Expect more of that.
Otherwise here are ten things I’ll be watching out for in the Budget statement and the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)’s report:

When Rachel Reeves sat down after last November’s Budget she was, rightly, chuffed at having doubled her fiscal headroom to £22 billion and reassured jittery markets. By this spring it had barely changed to £23.6 billion.

If you believe what has been widely speculated, or indeed The Spectator’s headroom tracker, increased government borrowing costs and expectations of interest rises have eroded it down to around £11 billion. If that proves true then will Healey use tax hikes and spending cuts to return it to more than £20 billion – or, as we’ve reported, might he think that a figure closer to £15 billion is enough?

The big surprise at the last Budget was that the ‘black hole’ never materialised and that headroom was a lot better than had been leaked. I think that could happen again. If it does it will be because wage growth and unemployment forecasts have been revised in a positive direction. Look out for them.

The other week the IMF gave Britain a pat on the back for being one of the only countries with serious plans to get rid of its deficit. But that assessment was based on tax and spending plans left by Rachel Reeves that no one considers credible. If they’re maintained they imply massive spending cuts right when the next election is due. Surely that’s not something any Labour government is actually going to deliver. If there is any extra money Healey will surely be tempted to address that.
Healey will also feel pressure to use any spare cash to get the ball rolling on defence spending given he resigned over our failure to do anything about reaching the new GDP target.

We already know one way Healey plans to increase defence spending is through capital investment in defence infrastructure. He hopes to achieve this while sticking to the fiscal rules. One wheeze that he will attempt to use are these so-called public financial institutions (PuFins) such as the national wealth fund and British business bank. The idea is that because the state takes on an asset as well as a liability then overall debt levels don’t change as judged by the rules. But I’m not convinced that’s true given that he’ll still need to go to the gilt markets for the initial outlay at a time when gilt yields remain very high.

I’ll of course have one eye on the gilt market. They’ll want to see credible plans that reduce borrowing but also tackle our baked-in inflation problem. If anything goes against that then Healey can expect an expensive reaction.

One leak we have had out of No. 11 is some sort of change to the income tax threshold so that the latest increase to the state pension does not drag pensioners whose sole income is the state pension into paying income tax. But how exactly will he achieve that? Will it be an age-based policy? Or a new threshold for everyone on low incomes?

The freezing of those thresholds has dragged lots more people – not just pensioners – into paying tax and they’ve dragged millions further up the tax bands too. These stealth taxes make up a huge part of the record high tax burden kicked off by the Tories and continued by this government. We’ll get new figures on just how much money that has raked in and how many of us it has affected.

The OBR has been repeatedly criticised for taking a too positive view of migration in terms of its fiscal costs and contributions. Will those assumptions be revised further today? Even if they’re not I expect a fall in their near-term forecasts for migration as the Boriswave reverses. That could also have an impact on headroom though it would likely improve GDP per capita.

The big economic surprise this year has been our GDP growth. The fastest in the G7 it has beaten most forecasts. Historically British growth tends to outperform in the first half of the year and then peter out as the year goes on. Do the OBR think that will happen again? Or, like the ONS, do they see the early shoots of AI boosting productivity and growth and what will that mean for their overall forecasts?

items.title: ASX ends flat as inflation boosts rate rise bets; tech stocks rally
paras: Advertisement Updated Business Markets World markets ASX ends flat as inflation boosts rate rise bets; tech stocks rally Staff writers Updated October 28, 2026 — 5:43pm , first published October 28, 2026 — 5:16am
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Share A A A The Australian sharemarket erased its morning gains after the release of the nation’s latest inflation figures increased pressure on the Reserve Bank to lift interest rates at its meeting next week.
The S&P/ASX 200 finished basically unchanged, down 2.8 points at 8847.30. Consumer spending-related stocks and energy stocks weighed on the market, although miners, banks and tech stocks advanced.

Wall Street was boosted by strength in technology stocks. Bloomberg Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed that headline inflation rose to 4.3 per cent in September from 4 per cent in August, due to a surge in petrol prices and a pick-up in the cost of building homes. The closely watched underlying measure of inflation was 3.6 per cent. This was up slightly from the August report, which had been revised down to 3.5 per cent. The bureau noted that petrol prices jumped by 9.4 per cent in September after a 14.8 per cent rise in August.
Meanwhile, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has made clear a further interest rate rise is on the agenda at the bank’s meeting on November 2 and 3.
Appearing before a Senate estimates hearing, Bullock said the nation’s fundamental economic challenge was the inability of the economy to grow without putting upwards pressure on inflation.
“Despite the unemployment rate recently rising a little more than we had expected, the labour market still seems a little tighter than we previously judged,” she said in an opening statement.
The back-to-back hawkish signals sent expectations for a rate increase next week to almost 90 per cent, while the yield on policy-sensitive three-year bonds climbed as much as 8 basis points.

“I think we can safely lock in a hike here,” said Robert Thompson, head of economics and rates strategy at Royal Bank of Canada in Sydney. “I would be shocked if the RBA didn’t lift rates given their rhetoric of late and the concerning detail in this report – core measures far too high, and key components lifting again.”

In currency markets, the Australian dollar strengthened to US70.31¢ on the news. It jumped as much as 1.9 per cent to $NZ1.26, its biggest intraday gain against the Kiwi in nine years, after the smaller nation’s central bank unexpectedly kept policy rates on hold, while the faster-than-expected inflation here is expected to force the RBA’s hand for a fifth rate rise this year.
Of the ASX’s 11 industry sectors, only the miners, banks and tech stocks finished the day in the green, while energy stocks and consumer-spending-dependent stocks posted the biggest losses.

Star Entertainment shares went into a trading halt ahead of a judgment by the Federal Court, which found the casino operator contravened anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing laws and hit it with a $260 million fine . Star argued in court last year that a fine of more than $100 million might be more than it can pay.

Justice Cameron Moore was damning about Star’s conduct, and acknowledged that the casino operator might need to raise further cash to pay the fine. “Star’s profitability is such that it is likely to need to raise money to pay any penalty,” he said.

Gold shares led the mining sector higher, although they pared back some of their gains in the afternoon, with Northern Star Resources finishing up 0.3 per cent, Evolution Mining up 2.2 per cent and Newmont up 0.5 per cent. Prices for the precious metal edged lower in the afternoon, testing the $US4000-an-ounce threshold and giving up some of the 1.1 per gain in the previous session ahead of the US Federal Reserve’s rate decision due on Thursday at 5am AEDT.
The two biggest miners, BHP and Rio, took a breather after their rally on Tuesday, inching up 0.1 per cent and 0.2 per cent. South32 rose 1.6 per cent and Lynas Rare Earths jumped 7.3 per cent.

Tech stocks posted the session’s biggest gains, shrugging off concerns about rising borrowing costs, thanks to renewed enthusiasm for artificial intelligence that lifted Wall Street overnight. Software makers WiseTech and Technology One added 1.5 per cent and 0.9 per cent, respectively, drone components maker Codan gained 2.9 per cent and cloud and data centre connections provider Megaport climbed 5.1 per cent.

Embattled NextDC, still recovering from its $3 billion share sell-off last week, rallied 9.4 per cent after outlining the contract conditions and financial covenants it has with its lenders and saying it was meeting those, with $8.67 billion in liquidity left at the end of September.

Consumer stocks struggled as investors braced for the probable next rate shock, which would mean Australians would pay even more for their mortgages and have less money to spend. Bunnings and Kmart owner Wesfarmers lost 2.1 per cent, JB Hi-Fi dropped 2.3 per cent, Harvey Norman fell 2 per cent and Rebel sports owner Super Retail Group lost 3.2 per cent.

Woolworths slipped 0.5 per cent despite saying its first-quarter sales rose 4.7 per cent to $19.4 billion, slightly beating market expectations. Rival Coles, which is releasing its first-quarter trading update on Friday, slid 1.2 per cent.

Meanwhile, three of the big four banks were trading higher, protecting the market from significant losses. CBA, the nation’s second-biggest stock, rose 0.6 per cent, Westpac gained 1 per cent, National Australia Bank was up 0.3 per cent and ANZ Bank finished flat.

The energy sector was the session’s biggest loser after a two-day drop in oil prices. Local oil and gas giants Woodside and Santos slumped 3.2 per cent and 1.7 per cent, while refiners Ampol and Viva Energy lost 3.8 per cent and 2.4 per cent, respectively.

They held on to their losses even as oil rebounded on a report the US may resume military strikes on Iran after next week’s midterm elections. Brent climbed towards $US116 a barrel after a two-day drop, while West Texas Intermediate was above $US101. The US has told several Persian Gulf nations to be prepared for a short, intense campaign, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing unnamed sources. President Donald Trump had not decided to go ahead, but was leaning towards a large post-election attack, the newspaper said.
“The market is pricing in a larger probability of re-escalation,” said Warren Patterson, head of commodities strategy at ING Groep.
On Wall Street overnight, renewed enthusiasm for artificial intelligence lifted equities ahead of earnings from some of the biggest tech companies and the Fed’s rate decision.

The S&P 500 rose 0.6 per cent and pulled within 1.2 per cent of its all-time high set this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 15 points, or less than 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.2 per cent.

Most stocks within the S&P 500 fell, but the gains for influential AI stocks made up for that. AI stocks rose to another winning day after swerving for weeks on worries about whether their boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips.

Broadcom climbed 4 per cent after announcing a $US63 billion ($89.6 billion) financing deal in which several Wall Street firms will help Anthropic get access to Broadcom’s XPU AI accelerators and networking solutions.
Elsewhere in the industry, Nvidia added 0.9 per cent. CoreWeave, a company that has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, jumped 7.9 per cent.

General Motors climbed 5.5 per cent after saying it is moving its stock from a listing on the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq. The carmaker said the Nasdaq, which is home to several of the world’s biggest technology stocks, is a fit for its tech-driven strategy.

Companies overall are under pressure to deliver big growth in profits. Expectations are high among investors, and that’s what allowed their stock prices to run to records recently despite high inflation, high interest rates and other concerns weighing on the market.
Boeing fell 10.7 per cent after reporting a larger loss for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

Hilton Worldwide Holdings sank 2.1 per cent after reporting weaker revenue for the summer than analysts expected. The hotel company said it expected to see “increased impact from the Middle East” during the quarter.

In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady a day before the Fed is scheduled to announce its latest rate decision. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged down to 4.99 per cent from 5 per cent late on Monday.

items.title: Abusive patients to pay for ambulance care under Labor election policy
paras: The Victorian Ambulance Union has welcomed Labor's proposal to charge abusive patients for ambulance services. ( ABC News )
Labor has pledged a crackdown on people who are aggressive towards Victorian paramedics if re-elected, including forcing patients to pay for ambulance care if they abuse or assault staff.
The move has been welcomed by Victoria's ambulance union which says more than half of its members were threatened with violence over the past year.
Advocacy groups, however, warn vulnerable people could be left without vital services.
The Labor Party says it will force abusive patients to pay for their ambulance rides if re-elected in Victoria next month.

Premier Ben Carroll announced an election commitment to crack down on patients assaulting or intimidating paramedics, stripping them of their Ambulance Victoria membership and charging them for the ride.
"If you assault a paramedic, if you threaten or intimidate a paramedic, it does not give you the right to have free public transport by that paramedic," Mr Carroll said.
Under the proposed system, abusive patients would have their membership revoked for 12 months, forcing them to pay costs of more than $2,000 for ambulance care.
Labor is promising to revoke the ambulance membership of anyone who shows aggression towards paramedics. ( ABC News )
The plan would come with a new patient charter devised by the government and Ambulance Victoria.
"When you pay your $56 for an Ambulance Victoria membership, you are signing up to a code of conduct," Mr Carroll said.
"If you are someone who has been a repeat offender or if you have actually acted out a violent episode with a paramedic, that would look at immediate suspension."
Ambulance Victoria would have the final say on whether a patient has been abusive and should have their membership revoked.
Mr Carroll said it should be left to medical professionals "who know their patients" to determine what constitutes abuse or intimidation.
The announcement comes amid a reported rise in attacks on first responders and paramedics.
The government said in the past year, 59 per cent of union members at Ambulance Victoria were threatened with violence and 28 per cent were assaulted.
Acting Victorian Ambulance Union secretary Olga Bartasek said the move was a welcome step to stemming a rising tide of violence.
"These things are just escalating and we need something to de-escalate," she told 774 ABC Melbourne.
"This year we've had a paramedic that was stabbed, that was one of the first ones here in Victoria.
"We had a member last week who had stitches in their head because they had been hit over the head with a bottle."
Australian Medical Association president Simon Judkins said there was no doubt there had been an increase in violence towards health professionals and that staff were entitled to a safe workplace.
"What has happened to our ambulance officers, to our nursing staff, to our doctors is unacceptable," he said.
But Dr Judkins said the policy would need to be carefully implemented to ensure people were not unfairly penalised.

"Patients who are have dementia or delirium, patients who have mental health conditions that haven't been properly addressed in community and end up in emergency departments, patients who have been there for 24, 48 hours and becoming unsettled," he said.
"We also want to ensure that those people who are vulnerable and still need access to care aren't unnecessarily impacted by some of these decisions."
The Victorian Alcohol and Drug Association is the peak advocacy body for treatment and support services.
Spokesperson David Taylor commended Labor's focus on protecting ambulance workers but said reducing access to healthcare for those with serious needs was problematic.

"For some folk who may well be unwell, whether with mental health issues or alcohol and drug or other things, they may not necessarily be able to grasp or be in a situation where they can consider the consequences of their actions," Mr Taylor said.
"So they wouldn't consider this policy when engaging in potentially inappropriate behaviour."
There are concerns the policy will deny healthcare to some who need help for things like drug addiction. ( ABC News: Robert Koenig-Luck )
"Let's say they're involved in a serious accident or something like that, are they actually really going to get turned away?

"If you're experiencing a significant level of disadvantage, to have that disadvantage exacerbated through reduced access to health services or financial penalties ... may be the inadvertent outcome from such a policy," he said.

items.title: Planned burns doubled and salvaged wood for sawmills under Coalition forest policy
paras: Danny O'Brien (middle) made the election pledge today with Vince Hurley (left). ( ABC News: Jarrod Whittaker )
Native timber would be processed at Victorian mills if the Coalition wins next month's Victorian election.
The Coalition said its forest management plan would increase cultural and planned burnings while working to reduce invasive pests and weeds.
A Gippsland timber mill has welcomed the news that milling could be revived.

Native timber from Victoria's bushland could be processed at local sawmills under a Coalition government as the opposition announces a suite of forest management pledges ahead of next month's state election.
Twice the amount of planned fuel-burning works would take place each year as part of the proposal.
The Coalition's forest management program would thin and reduce fuel loads across 5,000 hectares of public forest each year, which Nationals leader Danny O'Brien said would support regional jobs.
Timber harvested from state-managed bushland as part of forest restoration and fuel reduction programs would be processed at Victorian mills and used for sawlogs, firewood, biochar and mulch.
The pledge also included an expansion of cultural burns and a doubling of planned burns to address a recommendation from the Bushfire Royal Commission.
The Coalition said old-growth and hollow-bearing trees would be protected, while reducing the threat of invasive species and weeds.
It has also promised to invest $2.52 million across four years, partnering with industry on a $4.41 million bushfire detection camera network across eastern and western parts of the state.
Coalition spokesperson for public land management Melina Bath said the firebreak work under the management plan would produce logs for processing at local mills.
She said the closure of Victoria's timber sector had hurt regional communities, particularly in Gippsland and the state's north-east.

"This is about making sure that we actually manage the forest, that we treat the pests and weeds, that we provide the fire breaks … to ensure that firefighters can get in there when the wildfires come.
"And making sure that when there is timber … that we put it [to] its most high-value use and that we support local jobs here in Gippsland and in other areas of the state."
Planned burns would be increased as part of the plan. ( ABC News: Steven Schubert )
The Victorian government ended native timber harvesting in Victoria in 2024 , with the forestry transition program ending in June this year.
The Coalition's pledge to remobilise native timber processing follows One Nation's plan to revive native timber harvesting in Victoria.
Australian Sustainable Hardwoods (ASH) managing director Vince Hurley said the industry around Heyfield in Victoria's east had been calling for active forest management.
"Remember Heyfield's been impacted by bushfire three times in the last 25 years," Mr Hurley said.
"Having active forest management to enable bushfires to be controlled properly … is good for Heyfield and good for local communities, but it's also good for employment here."
He said using timber from native forest would benefit the community and consumers, many of whom purchased timber from interstate and overseas.
"They'll be able to buy timber that's produced locally in Victoria at a better price," Mr Hurley said.
Vince Hurley says it has been a tough time for the Victorian timber industry. ( Four Corners: Rob Hill )
He said the sector had faced headwinds since Victoria's native timber industry was closed.
"It's been very tough. We've had to source our timber from elsewhere," Mr Hurley said.

"We've had to buy operations in other states. We've had to go to the United States and buy raw materials out of the United States and manufacture in Australia. We've also had to spend a lot of money on capital works."
Environmental groups have pushed back on the Coalition's election pledge.
The Victorians for Nature alliance said the management program would face regulatory challenges, including court cases which have found native forest logging breached environmental laws.
The alliance is made up of the Victorian National Parks Association, Environment Victoria, the Wilderness Society and the Victorian Forest Alliance.
Victorian Forest Alliance spokesperson Nic Fox said logging native forest was "catastrophic for wildlife", particularly species such as greater gliders and powerful owls.
"Forests are worth so much more standing; providing clean drinking water, reducing erosion, carbon capture/storage, habitat and destination tourism," Mr Fox said.
"It is pointless to restart something with such low public support, and so many flaws, barriers and costs."
Jordan Crook says the policy is "logging wrapped in new branding". ( Supplied: Jordan Crook )
Victorian National Parks Association's nature campaigner Jordan Crook said the policy was "logging wrapped in new branding".
"But with the same ecological, hydrological and fire-increasing issues," he said.
"From examples around the world, we know the term 'active management' just means logging native forest."

items.title: Chalmers lowers hopes for fuel discounts after high inflation result
paras: Treasurer Jim Chalmers revealed headline inflation rose 4.3 per cent in the year to the month of September, compared to 4.0 per cent in August. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )
Jim Chalmers says the government's budget is not the main driver of inflation, but acknowledges today's figures are still "too high".
The treasurer has downplayed the likelihood of further fuel tax discounts, citing budget pressures.
The Reserve Bank is considered likely to hike interest rates when its monetary policy board meets on Tuesday.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers is urging "perspective", with today's disappointing inflation result making another rate hike a near certainty.

Facing fresh accusations from the opposition that a government "spending addiction" is putting pressure on inflation, Mr Chalmers repeated his longstanding insistence that the government's budget was playing "a helpful role" and was not a "primary driver".
"There are other factors at play," he told reporters today, naming the Middle East war and a surprising burst of private investment in data centres and other areas.

"For every five dollars of demand in our economy, four dollars [are] private and one dollar is public. I think that's an important bit of perspective when it comes to some of the commentary that is around today," he said.

"We've been able to manage the budget in a much more responsible way than it was being managed by our predecessors … We accept our part in the fight against inflation. We take responsibility for government policy when it comes to the fiscal settings."

Today's inflation figures confirm the glum prognosis of RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser, who last week warned that inflation was on track to be "materially worse" than the 3.5 per cent the bank forecast in August.
That forecast was for "underlying" inflation for the September quarter, the bank's preferred measure because it is smoother. The actual result was 3.7 per cent.

Economists responded by dialling up their expectations of a rate hike next Tuesday, which KPMG's Brendan Rynne called "locked and loaded" and Deloitte Access Economics' Stephen Smith called the "best bet on Melbourne Cup Day".

Markets also upgraded their expectations of a rate hike to 87 per cent next Tuesday, and fully "priced in" a hike by the end of the year, indicating a belief that a rate hike is a near-certainty in December, if not November.
Another rate hike of 25 basis points would take the rate to 4.85 per cent, its highest level since 2008.

The Coalition pursued the government over spending levels in Question Time and in Senate estimates today, where Treasury Secretary Jenny Wilkinson backed up Mr Chalmers' assessment that the budget was not a main driver.

"We can only control what we can control," she said, adding that recent budget updates had "taken some pressure from the government out of the economy" by consistently reducing the size of the budget deficits.
"We have seen public demand coming off … The thing that we have been surprised by has been that private demand in the economy has been stronger than we expected."
Jane Hume has repeatedly highlighted high government spending as contributing to inflation. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore )

Pressed by Liberal deputy Jane Hume about the overall level of government spending, which remains at levels rarely seen outside of recessions, Ms Wilkinson said it was important to consider the kind of spending, not just the overall amount.

A similar point was made by RBA Governor Michele Bullock, who maintained her policy of refraining from direct comment on the government's budgets, but named private sector activity, global pressures, and poor productivity as primary drivers of inflation.

"Continued weak productivity growth means that the economy cannot grow strongly without putting pressure on inflation. This is a fundamental challenge for the Australian economy and for everyone's real spending power over the next few years," she said.
Mr Chalmers downplayed any suggestion that the government would resume its fuel excise discount, despite the continue growth in fuel prices.
"We try to be up front with people and say we need to make sure that when we provide cost of living relief, it's not counterproductive.
"[We must] strike the most effective balance between the pressures on the budget, the pressures on people, and the pressures on our economy."
He labelled the Middle East war "disastrous for Australians, for cost of living, and … around the world" and said it was "absolutely turbocharging" inflation.
"From an economic point of view, the end of the war in the Middle East can't come soon enough."

Speaking in Question Time, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said economic difficulties were "not going to be solved overnight" but that the government would "continue to do everything we can to shield Australians from the worst of the impact."
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said government spending had made Australia "completely vulnerable to international factors" and reiterated calls for a fuel discount offset by further spending cuts.

items.title: Inflation jumps to 4.3%, adding to pressure for RBA rate rise next week
paras: EPA Inflation jumps to 4.3%, adding to pressure for RBA rate rise next week Published: October 28, 2026 12:24am EDT Australia’s annual inflation rate jumped to 4.3% in September , up from 4.0% in August, keeping pressure on the Reserve Bank ahead of Tuesday’s interest rate decision.
Market expectations for another rate rise next week – which would be the fifth this year – surged to 80% after the inflation report.

Petrol and holiday costs helped drive the increase. But the more important test for the bank was underlying inflation: the RBA’s preferred measure of quarterly inflation, the quarterly trimmed mean , rose 1.0%, up from 0.8% in June.

The headline consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.6% in September, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported . The biggest driver was automotive fuel prices, which jumped 9.4% in the month as world oil prices increased, leaving them 23.6% higher than a year earlier.

Domestic holiday travel and accommodation rose 8.0% in September, reflecting school holidays and major sporting events. These increases help explain the headline increase — without establishing that every part of the economy is overheating.

Housing inflation actually eased to 5.2% annually, down from 5.7% in August. New dwelling prices were unchanged over the month as builders’ discounts offset increases in base prices. Electricity prices remained 12.8% higher over the year, largely reflecting expired federal government rebates.

Higher petrol prices squeeze household budgets and raise businesses’ delivery costs. An interest rate rise cannot produce more oil, but it can slow spending across the economy and make it harder for businesses to pass on higher costs.

The underlying “trimmed mean” measure removes unusually large price rises and falls to give a clearer picture of the broader trend. It is the one measure the RBA pays the most attention to when setting interest rates.
On this measure, underlying inflation rose 1.0% in the September quarter. That quarterly increase matched economists’ expectations.
A quarterly pace of 1.0%, if sustained, would be well above the RBA’s 2–3% annual target. That is a warning about momentum, not a forecast.
The annual rate edged up to 3.7%, above the 3.6% forecast in a Bloomberg survey reported by Capital Brief .
Another possible complication is the removal of card payment surcharges . Visa, Mastercard and EFTPOS introduced no-surcharge rules on October 1.
Businesses still pay to accept cards. Some may recover those costs through higher advertised prices rather than a separate fee at the terminal.
A $5 coffee with a 10-cent card surcharge could become a $5.10 coffee without one. The card customer pays the same total, while someone who previously paid cash could pay more.
Read more: Are you seeing new ‘service fees’ since the card surcharge ban? Here are the rules
The RBA notes that payment surcharges are not included in the CPI. But if businesses build the costs into final prices, that would lift measured inflation.
In March, the Reserve Bank estimated that folding existing card surcharges into advertised prices could lift the consumer price index by around 0.1% .
This is not an extra 0.1 percentage points of inflation every year, nor an entirely unexpected shock.
An inflation surprise would require repricing beyond what forecasters had allowed for. On the other hand, lower payment costs and competition could limit increases.

The inflation report today covers September, before the rules changed. Businesses might have repriced in anticipation, but that remains a hypothesis requiring evidence. October will provide the first full month after implementation; higher cafe prices alone would not establish causation.
The figures add weight to the risk of another rate hike at the next RBA meeting on November 3, although quarterly underlying inflation matched expectations.
My own model of financial market data suggests that the odds of an interest rate hike have soared to 80% , compared with 56% earlier this week.
RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said last week the inflation outlook had deteriorated substantially relative to the bank’s August forecasts, citing energy prices and constraints on supply.

In a 60 Minutes interview broadcast on October 25, Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter described demand as too strong relative to supply. She warned about overseas cost increases becoming embedded in domestic inflation, while declining to speculate on the next RBA decision.
The cash rate is already at 4.60%, following September’s quarter-point increase. Those higher borrowing costs take time to restrain spending.

Persistent underlying inflation strengthens the case for further action. But the fuel-driven headline increase needs to be weighed against the more modest monthly underlying result and weaker consumption and rising unemployment, which were acknowledged by Hauser.
A hold would give the past four rate increases more time to work through the economy. It would not necessarily mean the tightening cycle was over.
The details of where the inflation is coming from, and the bank’s updated forecasts to be released next week as well, will matter more than the headline figures alone.
Read more: What exactly is inflation, and are interest rates the only option for dealing with it?

items.title: Hastings completes US$15M Thai rare earths plant deal

Share A A A Hastings Technology Metals has completed a 49 per cent acquisition of the Kabin Buri hydrometallurgical processing plant in Thailand, as the company fast-tracks its transition from miner to rare earths downstream producer.

The US$15 million (A$21.3 million) deal sees Hastings take a significant stake in the Thai facility’s owner, with a significant portion of the payment tied to performance. The consideration includes a previously paid US$0.5 million cash deposit and US$8 million in equity, to be satisfied through the issue of 23 million Hastings shares at an agreed price of 50 cents apiece to its partner, Enuo Holdings.

First feedstock shipment arriving at Hastings’ Kabin Buri hydrometallurgical rare earths plant in Thailand last quarter. A further US$1 million is payable as a commissioning payment, with the final US$5.5 million in deferred cash consideration payable only when contractual production and sales performance milestones are met.

The company says work is already progressing at the facility to upgrade its planned nameplate output capacity to 12,000 tonnes per annum of mixed rare earth chloride (MREC), representing a doubling of the plant’s originally contemplated throughput.
Hastings says testing and commissioning are on track to kick off in the first quarter, with first production expected to follow shortly after.

Importantly, the company says it has de-risked the plant’s start-up phase by securing a binding feedstock supply agreement with Enuo for a minimum of 10,000 tonnes per annum of monazite concentrate. The supply is expected to come from Africa, giving Hastings an independent source of feed while its flagship Yangibana project in Western Australia is brought online to potentially provide a longer-term runway for the plant’s initial years of operation.

Hastings Technology Metals chief executive officer Vince Catania said: “Completion gives us a clear run at construction and commissioning, with feedstock contracted. Our job now is to get on-spec product out of the door by Q2 2027.”

The acquisition accelerates Hastings’ mine-to-market strategy, transforming the Kabin Buri facility into a significant processing hub. The plant chemically cracks and leaches monazite concentrate into mixed rare earth chloride (MREC), an intermediate product for specialist rare earths separation plants.

It is one of the rare earth industry’s most technically demanding processing steps and, with only a handful of operators able to do it successfully, has become one of the sector’s biggest barriers to entry.

Based on management’s indicative estimates, the now-expanded plant could generate US$110.4 million (A$158M) in gross annual revenue and US$35.7 million (A$51.5M) in profit before tax at full capacity. Hastings’ share of that profit is forecast at US$15.5 million (A$22.35M) in the first full year of production, followed by US$17.5 million (A$25.2M) thereafter.

Looking ahead, Hastings has begun preparing an investment promotion application with Thailand’s Board of Investment (BOI). If successful, the promotion could allow the plant to be majority foreign-owned, opening the door for Hastings to increase its stake from the current 49 per cent. It could also provide significant tax incentives, including a corporate income tax exemption for up to 13 years.

By picking up a near-term production asset in Thailand, Hastings has found a shortcut to cash flow and skipped the long lead times that stall so many aspiring miners. Its Yangibana project remains the main event, but the Thai plant is a handy stepping stone towards a place among the world’s downstream players.

items.title: Strong inflation sets course for RBA to hike next week
paras: The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) has released Consumer Price Index (CPI) data for September 2026.
Headline CPI rose by 4.3% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 4.0% in the 12 months to August.
Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising by 5.2%.
Transport was the second-largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising 8.7% due to higher automotive fuel prices.
The policy-relevant trimmed mean annual inflation was 3.6% in September, up from 3.5% (revised) in August.
Using the pre-October 2025 methodology, quarterly trimmed mean CPI inflation was 1.0%, while annual trimmed mean inflation was 3.7% and continues to rise:
The annual result of 3.7% for the quarter was slightly above the 3.6% expected by economists and financial markets.

In her opening statement today to the Senate Economics Legislation Committee, Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) governor Michele Bullock took a hawkish tone on inflation and interest rates, tying the deterioration in the inflation outlook directly to re-escalating Middle East conflict and higher energy prices.

Bullock also said that inflation is likely to be higher than the RBA’s August base case, as some of the upside risks it flagged have materialised. She stressed that inflation is not only being imported, with elevated underlying inflation tied to domestic demand.
Bullock also said the labour market looks a little tighter than previously judged, even though unemployment has risen more than expected.
Weak productivity growth also means a longer period of subdued demand growth is needed to bring inflation down sustainably.

Looking ahead, Bullock said the RBA Board will assess the data and the balance of risks next week, with a key question being whether the tightening to date will be enough to return inflation to target in a reasonable time.
Given the firming of trimmed mean inflation shown above, the balance of probabilities suggests the RBA will hike again on Tuesday.

items.title: ASX pares gains as inflation figures put pressure on RBA
paras: Advertisement Updated Business Markets World markets ASX pares gains as inflation figures put pressure on RBA Staff writers Updated October 28, 2026 — 11:55am , first published October 28, 2026 — 5:16am
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Share A A A The Australian sharemarket has shed some of its morning gains after the release of the nation’s latest inflation figures increased pressure on the Reserve Bank to lift interest rates at its meeting next week.

Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed that headline inflation jumped to 4.3 per cent in September after being at 4 per cent in August, due to a surge in petrol prices and a pick-up in the cost of building homes.

Wall Street was boosted by strength in technology stocks. Bloomberg The closely watched underlying measure of inflation was 3.6 per cent. It was up slightly from the August report which had been revised down to 3.5 per cent. The bureau noted that petrol prices jumped by 9.4 per cent in September after a 14.8 per cent increase in August.
The S&P/ASX was up 38.4 points, or 0.4 per cent, to 8888.50 as of 11.52am AEDT, the bourse easing after the release of the inflation figures.
Meanwhile, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has made clear a further interest rate rise is on the agenda at the bank’s meeting next week.
Appearing before a Senate estimates hearing today, Bullock said the nation’s fundamental economic challenge was the inability of the economy to grow without putting upwards pressure on inflation.
“Despite the unemployment rate recently rising a little more than we had expected, the labour market still seems a little tighter than we previously judged,” she said in an opening statement.
Miners, banks and tech stocks powered the ASX this morning, while energy stocks declined. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.31¢.

Shares of Star Entertainment went into a trading halt ahead of a judgment by the Federal Court, which found the casino operator contravened anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing laws and hit it with a $260 million fine . Star argued in court last year that a fine of more than $100 million may exceed its financial means to pay.

Justice Cameron Moore was damning about Star’s conduct, and acknowledged that the casino operator may need to raise further cash to pay the fine. ”Star’s profitability is such that it is likely to need to raise money to pay any penalty,” he said.

Gold shares led the mining sector higher, with Northern Star Resources up 1.8 per cent, Evolution Mining up 3 per cent and Newmont up 1.1 per cent. Prices for the precious metal advanced as bargain hunters stepped in after it fell below a key level, while traders await the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate decision later this week.
“Gold is finding its feet again after briefly falling below $US4,000, with the sharp correction attracting bargain hunters and physical buyers,” said ING commodity strategist Ewa Manthey.

The two biggest miners, BHP and Rio, took a breather after their rally on Tuesday, rising 0.8 per cent and 0.6 per cent in early trade. Silver miner South32 rose 2.6 per cent, steelmaker BlueScope added 1.6 per cent and Lynas Rare Earths jumped 6.9 per cent.

Tech stocks also advanced, after renewed enthusiasm for artificial intelligence lifted US stocks ahead of earnings from some of the tech giants. Software makers WiseTech, Xero and Technology One added 2.4 per cent, 1.7 per cent and 1.4 per cent, respectively, drone components maker Codan gained 2.3 per cent and cloud and data centre connections provider Megaport climbed 6.8 per cent.

Embattled NextDC, still recovering from its $3 billion share sell-off last week, rallied 10.7 per cent after outlining the contract conditions and financial covenants it has with its lenders and saying it was meeting those, with $8.67 billion in liquidity left at the end of September.
AI data centre landlord Goodman Group rose 2.5 per cent, leading the property sector higher.

Woolworths, the nation’s biggest supermarket chain, rose 1.1 per cent after saying its first-quarter sales rose 4.7 per cent to $19.4 billion, slightly beating market expectations, with Australian supermarket sales up 6.9 per cent. Woolies’ sell-out Ooshies campaign, which ran from mid-July and was sold out in a month, was so popular that staff were at times unable to cope with the demands of higher foot traffic and sales, chief executive Amanda Bardwell said. Rival Coles, which is releasing its first-quarter trading update on Friday, slid 0.2 per cent.

Meanwhile, the big four banks were all trading higher, bolstering the market’s early gains. CBA, the nation’s second-biggest stock, rose 1.4 per cent, Westpac added 0.9 per cent while ANZ Bank and National Australia Bank advanced 0.6 per cent.

Energy stocks were lower as oil held its two-day decline, with traders tracking the outcome of a tight Israeli election that’ll help to shape the course of the US war with Iran. West Texas Intermediate traded near $US100 a barrel after falling more than 3 per cent in the past two sessions. Brent fell below $US114. In Israel’s election, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot edged ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in exit polls, though both blocs remain short of a majority and votes were still being counted.
Local oil and gas giants Woodside and Santos both slumped 2 per cent, and refiner Ampol lost 2.5 per cent.
On Wall Street overnight, renewed enthusiasm for artificial intelligence lifted equities ahead of earnings from some of the biggest tech companies and the Federal Reserve’s rate decision.

The S&P 500 rose 0.6 per cent and pulled within 1.2 per cent of its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 15 points, or less than 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.2 per cent.

The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 fell, but the gains for influential AI stocks made up for that. AI stocks rose to another winning day after swerving for weeks on worries about whether their boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips.

Broadcom climbed 4 per cent after announcing a $US63 billion ($89.6 billion) financing deal where several Wall Street firms will help Anthropic get access to Broadcom’s XPU AI accelerators and networking solutions.

Elsewhere in the industry, Nvidia added 0.9 per cent and was one of the strongest forces behind Broadcom pushing the S&P 500 higher. CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, jumped 7.9 per cent and was consistently higher through the day following several days of sharp swings.

General Motors climbed 5.5 per cent after saying it’s moving its stock from a listing on the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq. The automaker said the Nasdaq, which is home to several of the world’s biggest technology stocks, is a fit for its tech-driven strategy. The move could also allow GM to join the Nasdaq 100 index, which would force investment funds that mimic the index to buy it.

JetBlue Airways flew 19 per cent higher even though it reported a larger loss for the summer than analysts expected. CEO Joanna Geraghty said the company expects to return to making sustained operating profits next year and to deliver at least $1 in earnings per share in 2028.
Investors may have been bracing for something worse after the airline’s stock came into the day with a loss of nearly 48 per cent for the year so far.

Another travel company, Royal Caribbean Group, also helped lead the market and rose 5.5 per cent. The cruise operator delivered a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, while raising its forecast for profit over the full year.

Companies overall are under pressure to deliver big growth in profits. Expectations are high among investors, and that’s what allowed their stock prices to run to records recently despite high inflation, high interest rates and other concerns weighing on the market.
Boeing fell 10.7 per cent after reporting a larger loss for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

Hilton Worldwide Holdings sank 2.1 per cent after reporting weaker revenue for the summer than analysts expected. The hotel company said it expects to see “increased impact from the Middle East” during the quarter.

In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady a day before the Federal Reserve is scheduled to announce its latest decision on interest rates. The Fed last month hiked the fed funds rate for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing inflation, but the widespread expectation on Wall Street is that it will hold rates steady this time.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged down to 4.99 per cent from 5.00 per cent late on Monday.
Helping to keep yields in check was a drop for oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 1.2 per cent to $US109.41.
In other international markets, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. Stocks jumped 3.1 per cent in Seoul and fell 1.3 per cent in Shanghai for two of the bigger moves.

items.title: Breaking: Inflation surges more than expected ahead of RBA meeting
paras: The RBA deputy recently warned the inflation outlook was now "materially worse". ( ABC News: Sharon Gordon )
Australia's inflation rate picked up more than expected in September, increasing expectations of an interest rate hike next week.

The consumer price index rose to 0.8 per cent in the month, from 0.4 per cent in August, taking annual inflation to 4.3 per cent, up from 4 per cent a month earlier, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said.
"Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising by 5.2 per cent," ABS head of price statistics Rachael McCririck said.
The annual trimmed mean, a measure of underlying inflation, also picked up to 3.6 per cent in September. The August trimmed mean was revised lower to 3.5 per cent.
Last week, Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser warned the inflation outlook looked "materially worse" than the RBA had forecast, raising the prospect of another interest rate hike next week.
Market pricing put the chance of a November rate hike at more than 60 per cent ahead of today's inflation data release.
The RBA's interest rate setting board will kick off its meeting on Monday and hand down its decision on Tuesday afternoon.
It will also release its updated economic forecasts, including for inflation.

items.title: Reserve Bank holds 36 th Conference of State Finance Secretaries
paras: The 36 th Conference of State Finance Secretaries was held on October 27, 2026 at RBI, Mumbai. The theme of the Conference was ‘Role of Quality of Expenditure, Effective Cash and Prudent Debt Management in Enhancing States’ Fiscal Sustainability’. The Conference was attended by the Finance Secretaries of 27 States and three Union Territories as well as senior officials from the Ministry of Finance, Government of India, Controller General of Accounts and the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. Governor, Reserve Bank of India inaugurated the Conference. Addressing the participants, the Governor emphasised the importance of maintaining the quality of expenditure to ensure the long-term fiscal health of the States. He also emphasised on the need for the States to adopt prudent borrowing strategies and efficient cash management practices. The Governor urged the States to onboard onto the Unified Lending Interface (ULI) and utilise Programmable Central Bank Digital Currency (P-CBDC) for Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT). He also advised States to make effective use of the State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC) forum. During the Conference, the Governor released a Booklet titled ‘Compendium on Cash and Debt Management for State Governments’. The Booklet summarises relevant concepts, operational processes and good cash and debt management practices in a concise and accessible format. The meeting reviewed, inter alia, market borrowings by the States, short-term financial accommodation to the States from Reserve Bank, adoption of Benchmark Issuance Strategy by the States, etc. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1395

items.title: ED arrests six persons in cross-border drugs smuggling network
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): The Enforcement Directorate ( ED ) has arrested six persons in connection with an investigation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) case linked to a cross-border drug smuggling network, the agency said on Tuesday. ED 's Delhi unit arrested these accused in different operations launched on October 11, October 18 and October 20. The arrested accused are identified as Lovejit Singh alias Labba, Manjeet Singh alias Manna, Prabhjit Singh, Gurjot Singh, Ramandeep Singh, and Gurpreet Singh. "A major drug trafficking operation involving smuggling of heroin from Afghanistan into India was unearthed during investigation," said the ED in a statement. The PMLA investigation was initiated on the basis of seizure of 293.81 kg of heroin from containers imported by Sandhu Exports at Nhava Sheva Port by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence and seizure of 352.71 kg of heroin from two vehicles and a flat in Faridabad, Haryana, by the Delhi Police Special Cell. Thus, a total of 646.52 kg of heroin has been seized so far. ED investigation revealed that the arrested persons, Lovejit Singh, Manjeet Singh, Ramandeep Singh, Gurjot Singh, Gurpreet Singh and Prabhjit Singh, coordinated the smuggling, storage and distribution of heroin across Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi.

"These individuals were key members of a syndicate that smuggled heroin from Afghanistan and Iran, concealing them within shipments of talc stone and gypsum powder," said the ED . Accused persons incorporated Sandhu Exports, a front company owned by Prabhjit Singh, to carry out the smuggling of drugs, informed the federal agency. ED uncovered the highly sophisticated heroin smuggling and money laundering network where identification of multiple bank accounts, cash transactions, and operational expenses by the accused has been made. "Accused disguised the origin of the illicit funds, which were further layered and integrated into seemingly legitimate financial activities. It was also revealed that the syndicate did not make any payments to Afghan suppliers until the drugs were sold in local markets." Further, the agency said the accused used cash payments to purchase multiple vehicles including Toyota Fortuner, Etios and Hyundai Verna etc in second hand market for trafficking from the storage Hubs to further distribution. The ED investigation revealed that cash was used for the purchase of high-end smartphones and encrypted communication apps were used to coordinate smuggling activities. "Drugs smuggled from Iran and Afghanistan used to be imported via the Nava Sheva port in Mumbai, later stored at a rented godown in Shivpuri, Madhya Pradesh and further distributed for local supply in parts of Delhi, Punjab and Haryana. Transportation was carried out in lesser quantities of 10 kg to prevent detection by law enforcement agencies. Earlier, a property in Jandoli Village (Rajpura, Punjab), multiple bank accounts in the names of accused persons, and fixed deposits have been attached by ED ," added the agency. (ANI)

items.title: "No shortage of oil in world and prices should hopefully come down", says Hardeep Singh Puri
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Hardeep Singh Puri, Minister for Petroleum and Natural Gas on Tuesday said that there is no shortage of oil in the world and prices will come down soon, answering the question of the recent upswing in crude oil prices. Speaking to the media, the Union Minister cited global factors such as the war in the Middle East and voluntary cuts in oil production which are influencing the oil prices in the global market. He said, "It depends on global factors. One thing is very clear, there is no shortage of oil in the world...Today, more and more oil is coming on the market...There are other factors like geopolitical tensions. So, there is no shortage of oil but if there is tension in one part of the world, then the freight cost, and insurance freight cost will go up. Today, let us all hope that better sense prevails, that call for peace that our Prime Minister has been making from every forum...There is more than enough oil in the world and prices should hopefully come down. That's my expectation..." "If there's tension in one part of the world, then the cost of, if you have to take a longer route, then the cost of the freight cost, the insurance rate cost, that will go up...There's more than enough oil in the world, and prices should hopefully come down," he commented in his personal capacity.

The union minister said many countries such as Brazil, and Guayana among others are coming with their oil. Citing the stable prices in the last 3 years, the minister said that the government is taking every possible step to ensure stable oil prices. "Central government at every stage has stepped in to cushion and bring the prices down from November 2021 to May 2022. Now there are some global factors. The cost at the retail point is determined by the cost of the barrel in the international market plus the cost of transportation, freight, insurance, retailers, refining cost and margin, then dealers, margin, etc. We are solving all the problems we can, now you tell the global community to hold and bring them down," he added. This comes after oil prices rose nearly 2 per cent on Monday, reclaiming major losses from last week's sell-off. Brent crude features upped by $1.44, or 1.97 per cent in the afternoon. Earlier this month, Puri had said that the country is well-prepared to meet its growing energy demands, with a diverse range of oil sources. Speaking on the availability of oil in the global market, Puri emphasised that India has expanded its procurement base, moving from 27 suppliers to 39. (ANI)

paras: Join our Whatsapp channel PNN Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: The Mindfulness India Summit 2024, an initiative by the Mindful Science Centre, presented by HSBC and supported by CII Leadership and HR Committee, successfully concluded its two-day event on October 17 and 18, 2024, establishing new benchmarks in corporate culture and personal well-being. With over 40 international and national experts addressing mindfulness, emotional intelligence, and neuroscience, the summit highlighted how these principles are essential in transforming leadership, enhancing employee engagement, and fostering sustainable well-being within organizations. The evolving workplace landscape, particularly the increasing role of AI, requires a renewed focus on human-centric leadership and emotional resilience. The summit provided a platform for forward-thinking leaders to explore how mindfulness can effectively bridge this gap, ensuring both corporate excellence and employee well-being . The summit featured MasterChef Sanjeev Kapoor as the Chief Guest, who shared how mindful leadership has played a pivotal role in building his culinary empire. The Mindfulness India Summit 2024 has successfully proven that mindfulness is no longer a luxury but a necessity in modern corporate structures. items.title: Mukka Proteins Limited Announces Rs 98 Crore Preferential Issue for Acquisition and Expansion
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel VMPL Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: Mukka Proteins Limited , India's largest fish meal and insect meal producer and a leader in the animal protein industry , has announced the approval of a preferential issue worth Rs 98 crore by its Board of Directors. This strategic move will help Mukka Proteins in its ongoing domestic and international acquisition and expansion efforts, reinforcing its position in the global market. A significant portion of the funding will come from the promoter and promoter group, underlining their commitment to the company's robust growth strategy. The preferential issue will comprise up to 1.96 crore equity shares at Rs50 per share, aggregating to Rs98 crore. This price includes a premium of Rs49 per share on the face value of Rs1. Mukka Proteins will use the raised capital to enhance production capabilities and meet the growing global demand for sustainable and high-quality protein solutions, particularly in the fishmeal and insect meal sectors. In a clear show of confidence, Mukka Proteins' promoters have committed to a capital infusion of INR 60 crore through a preferential allotment of equity shares. This significant financial backing will be used to strengthen the company's financial position, reduce debt, and fund key operational improvements. Mukka Proteins has consistently embraced sustainability, having commercialized insect protein as a significant innovation for the aquaculture and animal feed industry. The company's waste-to-food initiatives have contributed to environmental sustainability, particularly in collaboration with the Mangaluru municipality for waste management. These efforts not only align with global environmental best practices but also enhance circular economy processes, focusing on converting municipal waste into valuable protein and oil products. Mukka Proteins is known for its strong commitment to ecological preservation, evident through the development of sustainable products such as fishmeal, fish oil, and insect protein. As a key player in the aquaculture and nutraceutical markets, Mukka contributes 25-30% of the market share in India's fishmeal and fish oil industry. The company plans to expand its operations further, capitalizing on this capital infusion to enter new markets and enhance its global footprint.

This issuance is subject to necessary statutory and regulatory approvals, including shareholder approval at the upcoming Extra-Ordinary General Meeting (EGM) on November 16, 2024. Managing Director and CEO Harris commented, "This preferential issue is a major milestone for Mukka Proteins as we continue to strengthen our market position. Our growth plans remain firmly rooted in sustainability, and this capital will enable us to scale up production, diversify our product offerings, and reinforce our commitment to responsible and eco-friendly business practices." Mukka Proteins Limited is poised to capture new opportunities in the animal protein sector, reinforcing its legacy of innovation, sustainability, and operational excellence. Mukka Proteins Limited : Mukka Proteins Limited is a leading manufacturer and exporter of fish meal , fish oil, and other protein products. The company has built a reputation for delivering high-quality, sustainable protein products to a global customer base. With a commitment to innovation and quality, Mukka Proteins serves industries including aquaculture, pet food, and agriculture across multiple continents. Headquartered in Mangalore, India, Mukka Proteins operates state-of-the-art processing facilities that meet stringent international standards. The company is dedicated to sustainable practices and has been at the forefront of environmental stewardship within the protein processing industry. items.title: Hon’ble Prime Minister of India inaugurates the Reserve Bank of India’s Data Centre and Cybersecurity Training Institute
paras: The Hon’ble Prime Minister of India, Shri Narendra Modi, today inaugurated the Reserve Bank of India’s newly established Data Centre and Cybersecurity Training Institute in Bhubaneswar, Odisha. This marks a significant milestone in strengthening the technological foundation of India’s financial system. Hon’ble Governor of Odisha, Shri Brajmohan Ram, Hon’ble Chief Minister of Odisha, Shri Mohan Charan Majhi; Hon’ble Union Finance and Corporate Affairs Minister, Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman; Hon’ble Union Minister for Tribal Affairs, Shri Jual Oram; Hon’ble Deputy Chief Ministers of Odisha, Shri Kanak Vardhan Singh Deo and Smt. Pravati Parida, and Hon’ble Members of Parliament, Shri Manmohan Samal and Smt. Aparajita Sarangi, also graced the event. 2. In his address, the Hon’ble Prime Minister highlighted the significance of the institutions inaugurated today - the Data Centre and the Cybersecurity Training Institute - in strengthening India’s digital financial infrastructure and advancing its technological self-reliance. The PM described the facility as a reflection of India’s changing approach to governance focused on taking the benefits of economic development to every region and every citizen. He emphasised that a secure banking system needs secure digital infrastructure supported by robust data centres and powerful computing systems and RBI’s new Data Centre is a critical step in this direction. 3. In her address, the Hon’ble Union Minister of Finance and Corporate Affairs underscored the strategic importance of resilient infrastructure in safeguarding financial stability and supporting sustained economic growth. She further said that the new Data Centre will house RBI’s mission-critical systems, including RTGS and NEFT, while the Training Institute will build expertise in cybersecurity, AI and other emerging technologies. 4. In his welcome address, Reserve Bank Governor Shri Sanjay Malhotra expressed gratitude to the Hon’ble Prime Minister for his participation in the event. He emphasised the Reserve Bank’s commitment to leveraging emerging technologies, strengthening digital infrastructure, enhancing cybersecurity, developing indigenous technological capabilities and supporting the country’s aspiration to become a developed nation by 2047. 5.
