items.title: The understanding that even bees have feelings is changing our view of consciousness
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print Bees seem to have surprisingly complex emotions Shutterstock/Qowi I recently discovered some scientific research that struck me to the core. I have spent many years exploring biology and the interconnectedness of life. Yet here was something that cut through all the knowledge I thought I had acquired: scientists have found that if male fruit flies are deprived of sex with females, they turn to alcohol . I immediately headed to the kitchen – not for a drink, but to watch some fruit flies I had seen earlier around a slice of lime my daughter had failed to clear away.

I took my hand lens, carefully snuck close to a Drosophila and peered into its red, mosaicked eye. We might be separated in evolutionary time by some 780 million years , I thought, but we share fundamental similarities. Natural selection has equipped us both with a brain that functions to improve our survival and that of our offspring. Is this why both flies and humans, on occasion, seek to douse flames of sexual rejection with alcohol? Just because flies don’t write poetry about it doesn’t mean they don’t experience a rich inner life.

My encounter with the fruit fly in the kitchen led me on a mission to understand the feelings experienced by other animals, including insects – to explore from a non-human point of view what it means to be conscious. Only a few decades ago, it was scientific taboo to suggest that even chimpanzees had personalities or feelings. Now, evidence of complex inner worlds in a wide range of non-human animals is mounting. Even “simple” animals make a good case. Fish seem to know themselves. Bees can be pessimistic. Cuttlefish plan for the future.

This is serious stuff, and it is incumbent on us to understand the extent of animal consciousness so that we can treat our fellow organisms with the respect they deserve. But the quest also sheds light on how this most murky and mysterious of attributes evolved, and what it actually means.

The big question is around what philosophers call phenomenological consciousness: having a subjective view of the world. The aptly named “hard problem” of consciousness is to explain not only why we have feelings at all, but to describe the physical basis of that subjective sense. Examining the lives of non-human animals can help tackle this notoriously difficult problem, says philosopher Tim Bayne at Monash University in Melbourne. “If we assume there is a kind of subjective experience in an animal,” he says, “what might it be like? What reason would it have to be conscious?”

I turn to Lars Chittka , a behavioural ecologist at Queen Mary University of London. His team’s work has shown that bumblebees engage in what can best be described as play . Chittka made a mini ball pit near the bees’ nest and found that the insects rolled the balls for extended periods. Not only that, but they seemed to enjoy it, going out of their way to go back to the play area. “It looks like subjective experience. It looks likely they are having emotion-like states,” he says.

Other insects seem to engage in play, too. Last year, researchers made an insect amusement park and found that some fruit flies sought out rides on a spinning carousel . Play is fun, but it has a function. In this case, perhaps the spinning motion helps the flies learn self-perception to fly and navigate better.

I asked Chittka about the haunting finding that male fruit flies drink alcohol if they can’t have sex. Flies that had recently mated and those that were prevented from doing so were both offered either regular food or food laced with 15 per cent ethanol. The sexually satisfied males ate both types equally, while the thwarted males strongly preferred the booze. The scientists also identified a neural system that links the rejection to the alcoholic reward. “For me, the observation that if you deprive male fruit flies of the opportunity to have sex, they turn to something that likely makes them feel better, it is highly suggestive that they are experiencing a negative feeling [that] can be remedied with a drug, in this case alcohol,” says Chittka.

You might object and say that neither play nor self-medication with alcohol is evidence of consciousness. Yet, to many scientists, the findings suggest there is a subjective sense of self held by these animals.

“I don’t know how to prove if another individual is conscious, even with humans,” says psychologist Nicola Clayton at the University of Cambridge. But she has tried to probe several animals’ subjective experiences. In one experiment, her team performed a version of the famous marshmallow test on cuttlefish, testing to see what the creatures would do when offered a choice between one treat (a live shrimp) immediately or two if they waited. Like some children, cuttlefish were able to delay gratification . “It’s an important part of planning for the future,” says Clayton. “I would say that’s good converging evidence that this animal has consciousness.”

A few years ago, when I visited Clayton’s aviary in Cambridge, I experienced something I can’t explain without endowing birds with consciousness. The aviary housed four or five young jays and, as Clayton opened the door and we entered, the birds first came to see her, but then, on seeing me, a stranger, they ran behind a nest box as if to hide. The birds started vocalising – it sounded like they were saying: “sorry – sorry!” I looked to Clayton in astonishment. “They are apologising for running away. It’s because they don’t know you,” she said.

This instinctive interpretation may be hard to prove, but Clayton and her colleagues have shown that jays can relive past moments and anticipate future ones. In one 2024 experiment, food was hidden under one of a line of distinctive cups. The watching jay was then removed while the order of the cups was shuffled. When the bird returned to the test chamber 10 minutes later, it could remember the correct cup . This is good evidence for episodic memory – long-term, event-based memory – and is evident in the wild: jays have evolved to cache food and retrieve it later, and adjust their behaviour to deceive others if they are being watched.

As I assimilate this new thinking on animal consciousness, I find myself moving through the world in a different way. I notice some honeybees landing on cyclamen flowers, and watch the bees carefully for signs of caution. Chittka has shown that if bees encounter crab spiders lurking in flowers, they become nervous when visiting other plants .

That makes sense, because crab spiders are dangerous predators of bees. “Their demeanour changes – they fly slower,” says Chittka, “but false alarms happen.” They will sometimes check out a flower that has no predator, yet still reject it. “It’s as if they’ve seen a ghost,” says Chittka. “Anthropomorphically speaking, it’s like we see in PTSD when people conjure up a threat of something not there.”

Bees aren’t the only seemingly simple creatures with signs of consciousness: the more experiments scientists conduct, the more they uncover animals with complex inner lives. Magpies are one of a growing number of species to have passed the mirror test , and were the first non-mammals shown to do so. This test aims to assess whether an animal has a sense of self based on its interaction with its own reflection. Perhaps it’s not too surprising that a magpie can do this, but more startling is the finding that a fish – the cleaner wrasse – has also passed the mirror test .

Will Sowersby at the Arthur Rylah Institute in Australia and his colleagues noted the speed and ease with which cleaner wrasse habituated to a mirror in their tank and started using it to inspect their own bodies. But then they saw a fish take a piece of shrimp, drop it in front of the mirror, and watch it fall in the reflection. It was as if the fish was a kind of physicist, performing an experiment. “What we were seeing is evidence that an animal can undertake hypothesis testing,” says Sowersby. “The cleaner fish used a piece of shrimp to test the properties of the mirror. A remarkable observation.”

Sowersby’s colleague Shumpei Sogawa at Osaka Metropolitan University in Japan is more measured. “What is particularly striking,” he says, “is that such behaviour can look extraordinary to us because we tend to underestimate what fish normally do.”

Amid the various tests, animals’ ability to learn from experience is increasingly considered one of the most important signifiers of consciousness. Jonathan Birch , a philosopher at the London School of Economics, has been working with neurobiologist Simona Ginsburg and geneticist Eva Jablonka on a framework they call unlimited associative learning , or UAL. To evaluate consciousness, they propose measuring five aspects of an animal’s capacity to learn.

One important aspect is the ability to learn to associate one stimulus with a second, novel stimulus. The classic example is Pavlov’s dogs: the canines learn to associate a bell with food, then they salivate at just the sound of the bell. Fruit flies and honeybees can do this, so these animals, and dogs, tick that box in the UAL checklist. This sophisticated learning reflects animals’ consciousness, says Birch. “Animals are not just calculators. They don’t just solve puzzles. They also have emotions. They have inner lives in which they feel things, and we can make inferences about these things as well.”

Birch, Ginsburg and Jablonka have combed through the scientific literature to build the case for UAL, and therefore consciousness, in a range of animals. Their work suggests consciousness independently evolved at least three times, says Birch: in vertebrates, where it led to consciousness in birds and mammals; in cephalopod molluscs, where it led to sentient octopuses and cuttlefish; and in arthropods, which created conscious insects, spiders and crustaceans, such as lobsters. “In at least those three lineages, they’ve gone from a non-conscious starting point to having a form of consciousness,” says Birch.

What we are learning from animals helps sharpen the thinking on why consciousness evolved, says Bayne. “The basic purpose of consciousness is to alert you to critical bodily needs: do I need food? Am I too hot? Am I too cold? Am I in danger? Is this a mating opportunity?” he says. If the purpose of consciousness is to address those variables, then it makes sense why bodily sensations like thirst are so vivid and salient, and so central to consciousness.

The advantage of UAL is that it doesn’t get bogged down in some bigger grand theory for the mind, such as integrated information theory or global workspace theory. “You say, ‘I don’t care about theories of consciousness. I’m just going to look for behavioural and neural signatures of consciousness and see if they’re similar to what happens in humans,’” says Anil Seth at the University of Sussex, UK.

These approaches avoid directly trying to answer the hard problem of why a physical process is accompanied by a conscious feeling. “I don’t think we make the best progress by going after the hard problem directly,” says Seth. “I think we go after it indirectly, and this is one way of doing that.”

“We don’t need to solve the hard problem to have evidence of consciousness in other systems,” says Birch. “Indeed, it might lead over the longer term to better solutions, because the more evidence you have, the better position you’re in to develop theories about the nature of consciousness.”

These recent discoveries in animals raise some serious questions about welfare. “What I hope is that the growing awareness of there being a kind of inner life in many animals, including invertebrates like octopuses, does lead to changes in the way people treat them,” says Birch. We have seen this in the opposition to octopus farming. “People have seen [that] octopuses are these amazing beings with rich mental lives,” he says. “It’s inappropriate to pack 20 or 30 of them into tiny spaces.”

The key question for whether we have a right to exploit an animal, says philosopher Simon Brown at Ashoka University in Sonipat, India, is “whether they have genuine interests where you can do things that matter to them, in the sense that they have a perspective from which certain things are good or bad for them”.

It seems there is a strong case that insects, spiders, lobsters and crabs, as well as fish, cephalopods and all vertebrates, have this self-perspective. Insects such as crickets and black soldier flies are raised in their billions to be processed for food, mainly for animals , with next to no thought for their inner lives. “They are killed by microwave,” says Chittka. “We can do better, though, and minimise suffering.”

I thought back to my close encounter with the fruit fly in the kitchen. Insect compound eyes are constructed such that a black dot called a pseudopupil can appear when you look at the eye head-on. This had the unsettling effect, when I peered at it with my lens, of making it seem like the fly was gazing intently into my eye. Drosophila has been the subject of countless experiments. As well as hitting the booze, males prevented from mating exhibit various responses, such as enhanced aggression, that scientists describe as “frustrative-like” . This can’t help but give you an insight into what it is like to be a fly.

“Knowing that about Drosophila changes, at some level, your appreciation of the kind of thing it is, and gives you access to it,” says Bayne. “Many people would take very seriously the idea that insects are conscious.”

Billions of individual flies, maybe trillions, have been bred and investigated and mutated, with little or no regard for their welfare. This sends a shudder through me, and I hope it does you, too. And even with an awareness of the danger of anthropomorphising them – male fruit flies aren’t like men in their taste for alcohol – it is hard to deny that there is something wonderful and unifying about what we are learning about the feelings and inner lives of our fellow creatures.

items.title: How vaccines could be about to revolutionise acne treatments
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print Can we prevent acne by targeting proteins released by C. acnes bacteria? Science Photo Library / Alamy It’s a cruel twist. Just as we become more concerned about our appearance, our faces start to erupt in great red spots. Pimples cause anguish for many teenagers and can persist into adulthood too. But now two companies are developing vaccines that they hope will revolutionise the treatment of acne. Is an end to the misery at hand?

The main idea behind this new approach is that acne is caused by the immune system overreacting to proteins released by skin bacteria. Triggering the body to produce antibodies against these proteins should block this process and prevent – or at least reduce – acne. Pharma giant Sanofi is preparing for trials in the US and Canada of an mRNA vaccine targeting at least one bacterial protein, while US start-up Armora Biosciences is focusing on a different protein.

Better treatments for acne are certainly needed. “Acne causes a significant emotional burden,” says Tomasz Zastawny at Armora. “It can lead to the development of depression, social isolation and other psychological outcomes as well.”

It has been known for decades that acne is linked to the presence of a bacterium called Cutibacterium acnes , which thrives deep in hair follicles where there is little oxygen. But C. acnes is the most common skin bacterium, present on just about everybody – including those that don’t have acne – so there’s a lot more to it.

One factor is the surge in hormones during puberty, which increases the production of fatty substances in the skin, affecting bacterial growth. But not everyone gets pimply during adolescence, so there seem to be genetic factors involved as well.
“Acne is very complicated. It’s not an infection,” says Richard Gallo at the University of California, San Diego. “It’s an immune problem.”

In other words, while the presence of C. acne doesn’t usually cause problems, sometimes it may trigger a strong immune response inside a follicle. During this response, some cells in the skin actually turn into fat cells and start releasing alarm signals and antimicrobial substances – a process known as reactive adipogenesis. “This is a normal way to fight an infection, but in this case, it’s an inappropriate response,” says Gallo.
What triggers that response? C. acnes can secrete a toxin known as Christie-Atkins-Munch-Petersen factor, or CAMP. The bacteria may ramp up production of CAMP in certain circumstances.
So, Gallo’s team tried vaccinating mice against CAMP, to make the animals produce antibodies that neutralise the toxin. A number of studies by his team suggest this could help prevent or treat acne .

Sanofi has now developed an mRNA vaccine that targets CAMP, possibly along with some other C. acnes proteins – the company hasn’t revealed exactly what’s in the vaccine and, after much back and forth, declined to talk to me about it.

While there have been reports that the Sanofi trial is already underway, it is labelled as “not yet recruiting” as per the latest update on 18 September. This means it may be some time before we know if it works. That said, while these initial trials are primarily intended to establish safety, it should be clear to volunteers within weeks if it is making a difference to their acne – this isn’t like a normal vaccine trial where researchers have to wait months or years for people to be exposed to pathogens.
“We were very, very optimistic that this could be revolutionary for acne therapy,” says Gallo. “We’ll just have to see if it pans out in the human population.”

Meanwhile, Armora is targeting a different protein, called hyaluronidase, based on work by George Liu at the University of California, San Diego. Hyaluronidase is an enzyme that breaks down hyaluronic acid, a large sugar secreted into the spaces between cells. These terms might be familiar because hyaluronic acid is often used as a filler for cosmetic purposes, while hyaluronidase is injected to break down filler that is no longer wanted or if things go wrong.
We are finally working out what happens to the skin and gut microbiome when someone gets acne, giving us new targets for treatments

Some bacteria such as strep B ( Streptococcus agalactiae ) produce hyaluronidase for similar purposes, to help them invade tissues. There are two main types of hyaluronidase, it turns out. Some break down hyaluronic acid into simple sugars. Others break it up into large chunks that act as an alarm signal to the immune system.

When it became clear that there were two types, Liu’s team searched genetic databases to see which type is found in which bacteria. They found the “simple sugars” type was the most common. The “large chunks” type was limited to a few free-living bacteria, which makes sense because they don’t need to worry about immune systems.

“The exception was acne,” says Liu. C. acnes jumped out to the researchers because it produces both types of hyaluronidase. More precisely, some strains of C. acne produce the simple-sugars type, while other produce the large-chunks one – none produce both, he says.

That made Liu wonder if this was connected to acne. Sure enough, the team showed in mouse studies that large-chunks strains of C. acnes cause acne-related inflammation, while the simple-sugars one slightly reduces inflammation. The team then went to show that a vaccine that stimulates the production of antibodies targeting only the large-chunks form of hyaluronidase could reduce acne in mice, as could inhibiting the enzyme with a small protein.
What isn’t clear is why some strains of C. acnes have evolved to trigger an immune response. One possibility is that it is a way to kill off some of their competitors, says Liu.
He thinks that in people, a vaccine against the large-chunks form of hyaluronidase would be most effective against the “more severe, red, angry type of acne lesion”.
“The ones that are hard to treat right now, those are the ones that we would target with a vaccine,” he says.

His findings might also help explain why antibiotics, which are commonly prescribed for acne, don’t work that well: they kill off the helpful C. acnes strains as well as the harmful ones. The other issue with antibiotics, of course, is that resistance can develop.

Another acne treatment called isotretinoin (Roaccutane) is more effective than antibiotics but has a long list of nasty side effects including causing birth defects, impotence and dry, itchy skin. How it works isn’t clear, though there is some evidence it alters the skin microbiome .

Acne vaccines promise to solve all these issues. They shouldn’t have any lasting side effects, nor should there be any issue with resistance, because the vaccines are targeting secreted proteins rather than directly targeting bacteria.

The fact that two competing approaches are being developed is great news for those with acne. If one vaccine doesn’t work, perhaps the other will. And it could be that both will work, or that targeting both CAMP and hyaluronidase simultaneously will prove even more effective than either alone. Maybe, just maybe, adolescence is about to get a little easier.

items.title: Major greenhouse gases rise again to record levels
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print The world is failing to rein in greenhouse gas emissions Yuri Turkov/Alamy The three main greenhouse gases reached unprecedented concentrations globally in 2025, continuing an upward trend that will lead to more global warming, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) warns.

The WMO Global Atmosphere Watch programme has published its annual bulletin on the amount of greenhouse gases that have accumulated in the atmosphere, ahead of the UN’s COP31 climate conference, which will be held in Turkey in November.
It reports that the global average surface concentration of carbon dioxide reached a record 426.8 parts per million (ppm) in 2025, which is 53 per cent higher than pre-industrial levels.
The increase from 2024 to 2025 was slightly higher than the average annual growth rate over the past decade, but the increase wasn’t as steep as the previous year.

The levels of methane and nitrous oxide also reached record highs of 1948 parts per billion (ppb) and 339.1 ppb respectively in 2025, an increase of 167 per cent and 26 per cent on pre-industrial levels.

“Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies,” WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett said in a statement.

This follows the UN recently confirming that the global target to limit warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels is due to be exceeded in the next few years , with emissions on track to cause 2.8°C of warming by the end of the century.

The WMO report also warns that more attention should be given to the steadily rising levels of two other gases in the atmosphere, molecular hydrogen and sulphur hexafluoride, as more countries decarbonise their energy systems.
Although hydrogen isn’t a greenhouse gas, it has a strong indirect effect on global warming and is being used for energy storage. Its concentration increased by 5.3 per cent between 2010 and 2024.

Sulphur hexafluoride, used primarily as a spark suppressant in electricity distribution, has the highest 100-year global warming potential overall – approximately 24,000 times that of CO2. According to the WMO, levels have been increasing steadily over the past three decades in proportion to growing global electrification.

items.title: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
paras: MIT Technology Review The Big Story Artificial intelligence Biotech & health Climate & energy 10 Breakthrough Technologies AI Hype Index The Impossible issue Menu MIT Technology Review MIT Technology Review The Big Story Artificial intelligence Biotech & health Climate & energy 10 Breakthrough Technologies AI Hype Index The Impossible issue Climate change and energy How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid.

Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade.

As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers. New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure.

Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits. Solid-state models, in comparison, combine magnetic components with high-power semiconductors, making them more compact and allowing for more control over the flow of electricity.

These devices are still in development, and can’t replace all traditional transformers today, especially the largest ones that work at the high voltages necessary for long-distance transmission. But a new generation of transformer technology could be a crucial part of our future grid.

Moving electricity through the grid isn’t perfectly efficient: As electricity flows through power lines, some gets lost as heat. How much varies—the higher the voltage, the lower the current, and the less electricity gets lost. So a key function for the grid is stepping voltage up and down.

Consider, for example, your local solar plant. For that electricity to efficiently travel to your home hundreds of miles away, it needs to reach a higher voltage than what’s generated by the solar plant. Enter transformers.

In its path from the power plant to your outlets, electricity might go through one transformer at the solar farm and another at a substation nearby, stepping up the voltage twice to reach a high enough level to travel on high-voltage transmission lines. Solar panels also produce direct current (DC) electricity, which needs to be converted to alternating current (AC) via an inverter before it flows into a transformer. Closer to its destination, the voltage will be stepped down again, probably at least twice: once at another substation and again at a smaller transformer in your neighborhood.

If you’re in the US, electricity from a solar plant might be converted to AC by an inverter at around 480 volts, get stepped up to 115,000 volts for the transmission lines, and finally get stepped back down to 120 volts and 240 volts for your home.

Conventional transformers do this work using what essentially amount to loops of wire. The core of a transformer is typically made of a special type of steel called grain-oriented electrical steel. Coils of copper wire sit on either end of that core.

The number of loops in each coil determines the voltage on either end of the transformer: If there are more loops on the secondary coil than the primary, the voltage steps up, and if there are fewer, it steps down. When incoming electricity passes through loops on the upstream end of the transformer, that forms a magnetic field in the core. That field induces a voltage in the loops on the other side of the device, which is what allows the energy to continue flowing at a new voltage. This process is called magnetic induction.

Transformers form the backbone of electricity transmission and distribution, says Srdjan Lukic, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at North Carolina State University. In addition to doing the job of stepping up and down voltage, transformers also often provide what’s called galvanic isolation, meaning there’s no direct electrical path flowing through them. That can help limit disturbances from moving through the grid, improving safety.
The problem is that today’s transformers are big and bulky, and they’re also difficult and expensive to replace, Lukic says.
Solid-state transformers essentially add so-called power electronics—semiconductors that convert and control electricity to the typical blueprint of today’s transformers.

While a conventional transformer operates at the frequency of the part of the grid it’s connected to, a solid-state transformer actually controls the frequency of the current. Typically, a solid-state transformer first converts incoming AC power from the grid to DC power, and then to a higher-frequency AC power using switches made of a semiconductor like silicon carbide.

From there, a magnetic component changes the voltage. Because the advanced semiconductors allow transformers to exert so much control over the frequency and stability of the current, the magnetic core can be much smaller than in a conventional transformer. Some come in at roughly one-tenth the size but have the same capacity, Lukic says.
Finally, additional power electronics convert the electricity from high-frequency AC to its required form—generally back to DC power and finally to lower-frequency AC.

Today, stepping voltage up and down is many transformers’ only job. But solid-state transformers can do much more. They absorb the jobs of devices like rectifiers and inverters (which convert AC to DC power and vice versa), shrinking the total footprint of the electrical equipment and potentially cutting the amount of power lost in the system.

In August, the New York Power Authority and the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) tested a one-megawatt solid-state transformer under realistic utility conditions at EPRI’s test site. The device was built in Lukic’s lab, and it was the first such test for a transformer of that capacity, he says.

The prototype was roughly 98% efficient—meaning it lost only 2% of the energy fed in. An equivalent conventional transformer and rectifier, by comparison, would be about 96% efficient together, Lukic says. A difference of 2% might seem small, but it is significant, since it means the solid-state transformer could cut power losses from conventional equipment in half, Lukic says.

One major goal of the project was to help utilities gain more confidence in these new components, Lukic says. That’s crucial, since these devices could be used on the power grid in the future. In the near term, solid-state transformers could be used within data centers to provide electricity for server racks.

The prototype is still a relatively low-voltage system, operating at about 15,000 volts. Industrial facilities like larger data centers often require higher-voltage connections, and transmission lines typically operate at hundreds of thousands of volts. Adapting solid-state transformers to these higher voltages will require further engineering development. But the test was a successful demonstration that solid-state transformers can work under real conditions, Lukic says.

Companies developing solid-state transformers are largely focused on data centers right now, Lukic says. There’s an influx of money to support developing the new technology, and the voltage requirements aren’t as high as they will be for larger transformers that will be needed for long-distance transmission.

In February, Heron Power raised $140 million to commercialize its solid-state transformer, which the company calls the Heron Link. The technology could be used in data centers, solar power arrays, and grid batteries, says Drew Baglino, the founder and CEO. The company is starting to test its technology at larger scales now, Baglino says. Ten megawatt-hours’ worth of batteries at Heron’s headquarters in Scotts Valley, California, will soon undergo testing with Heron transformers. The company is also planning a pilot with a nearby solar farm, Baglino says.

One challenge for solid-state transformers is that their power electronics have more failure modes than conventional transformers. In a traditional device, a failure means that the entire device will typically be taken offline, resulting in power interruptions. But Heron designs with that in mind, Baglino says: The company uses a modular design, with many small devices that work together. If one fails, the rest of the system keeps working until the affected bit can be replaced, which doesn’t require shutting the whole thing down.

Heron Power is currently building a $100 million factory in California to make advanced transformers. The facility should begin production in 2027 and reach its full production rate of 40 gigawatts’ worth of transformers per year in 2029.

In recent years, companies that make grid equipment have put $1.7 billion into the US supply chain for power transformers, which are used in high-voltage transmission, says Benjamin Boucher, a supply chain analyst at Wood Mackenzie. There’s been an additional $1.3 billion invested for distribution transformers, the smaller devices that help transform power for homes and businesses, he adds.

But even this investment isn’t keeping pace with the rapid growth of the grid. Wait times for large conventional transformers—the kind needed to connect new power plants, long-distance transmission, and high-demand sites like data centers—are stretching as long as five years.

“Transformers have become one of the biggest bottlenecks for utilities, generation developers, and even data centers,” Boucher says. The big challenge is that it’s difficult to get new transformer manufacturing up and running, because it’s a quite technical process that requires a lot of specialized labor. So even facilities announced years ago are still years from opening, Boucher says.

Solid-state transformers could help ease some of that pressure. But high-voltage devices needed for power plant connections and transmission lines are the holy grail for solid-state transformers, Lukic says. Existing solid-state technology can’t be used for those applications yet, so the industry will need to develop new materials and designs to support high voltages and handle electricity safely in a compact device.
“We’re facing a big risk related to grid infrastructure,” Boucher says. “Without the transformers, you don’t really have an electrical grid.”

items.title: Microsoft offers to buy out a quarter of its workforce
paras: Buyout Bonanza Microsoft offers to buy out a quarter of its workforce Employees in the US, Canada, India, and the UK may receive offers to leave MS today.

122 Credit: Drew Angerer | Getty Images Credit: Drew Angerer | Getty Images Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav On Monday, Microsoft said it will offer voluntary buyouts to eligible employees in select parts of the company. CNBC reports that the buyouts will be offered to roughly 60,000 employees , or about a quarter of its global workforce. The company describes the offer as an opportunity for employees who may have already been considering career moves outside Microsoft. While Microsoft did not give a direct reason for the buyout package, it comes as the company has spent the last several years managing costs amid investment in AI infrastructure and data-center buildout.

Microsoft will extend the voluntary exit offer (VEO) to qualifying employees in the United States, India, Canada, and the United Kingdom. Microsoft employees at level 70 or below will be eligible for the buyout program. The company’s employee rankings are internal, but according to the salary and career database Levels.fyi , levels 65–67 correspond to principal positions, and 68–70 are at the partner/distinguished level. According to Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, eligible organizations were selected “based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs.”

The effort is the second time Microsoft has run a voluntary workforce reduction in 2026. In April, the company offered its first voluntary retirement package to 8,750 US employees. In July, the Xbox division laid off 3,200 employees , or about 20 percent of its entire gaming division. As reported by CNBC , about 30 percent of eligible employees accepted the retirement offer, lessening the impact of the planned layoffs, according to Coleman. While the offer in April went out to long-tenured employees who might be nearing the end of their career, the VEO expands the effort to a much larger potential pool.

In comments to GeekWire in July, Coleman said Microsoft was looking into making voluntary exits part of workforce management more regularly. She described the current VEO as something that “builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program.”

While layoffs remain the most common way to reduce headcounts in the tech world, Microsoft may be following Google’s playbook. As Business Insider reported, Alphabet offered employees voluntary exit packages in June and October 2025, and again in February 2026. Now, eligible Microsoft employees may have to decide whether to take a deal now or keep their jobs and face the uncertainty of future company-wide layoffs.
According to Microsoft’s blog , employees eligible for the VEO will be contacted via email on Monday. Microsoft will announce its latest earnings after market close later this week.

items.title: Stan Wawrinka: The Other Swiss Tennis Great From The Big Four Era
paras: Trying to make your name in a sport dominated by a select few players was a challenge Stan Wawrinka seemed to relish. The Big Four were Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal, Andy Murray, and Novak Djokovic.
Between 2004 and 2023, they won 69 of the 79 Grand Slams held. During this period, only one player outside of the quartet won a major three times – Wawrinka.

On his way to the 2014 Australian Open title, he defeated both Djokovic and Nadal, as well as three other seeded players. The following year, he defeated Federer and Djokovic to win the French Open. Then, at the 2016 US Open, he beat Juan Martin del Potro, Kei Nishikori, and Djokovic in consecutive matches. In his prime, Wawrinka established himself as a player who thrived on the biggest courts in the world.

Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
